turns.question: Our groundwater well pod is showing turbidity of 12 NTU. Is that too high for our pod?
turns.answer:
The pod’s configured turbidity threshold isn’t available here, so I can’t say whether 12 NTU exceeds a specific limit for this deployment.  

For context, the USGS notes that “natural turbidity in ground water generally is less than 5 turbidity units”【1†"natural turbidity in ground water generally is less than 5 turbidity units"】, but also that “Natural ground‑water turbidity of up to 19 turbidity units has been reported”【1†"Natural ground-water turbidity of up to 19 turbidity units has been reported"】.  

Thus, 12 NTU is higher than the typical natural background but falls within the range that has been observed in some groundwater settings.

-- 40 of 55 --Chapter A6. Field Measurements 	Turbidity, Version 2.1 (9/2005)
TBY—41
e. 	Report turbidity as follows, using method codes as described
in http://water.usgs.gov/owq/turbidity_codes.xls (accessed
9/30/2005)5:
• For EPA Method 180.1, use NTU or NTRU.
• For GLI Method 2, use FNMU.
• For non-diluted, non-USEPA-compliant measurements, use
the reporting units described in table 6.7–4.
In contrast to surface waters, natural turbidity in ground water
generally is less than 5 turbidity units. Natural ground-water turbidity
of up to 19 turbidity units has been reported for some environmental
settings (Nightingale and Bianchi, 1977; Strausberg, 1983; Puls and
Powell, 1992). Contaminated ground-water systems, however, can
have considerably higher turbidity (Wells and others, 1989;
Gschwend and others, 1990; Puls and Powell, 1992; Backhus and
others, 1993). Measuring turbidity in ground water requires special
considerations and procedures. For effervescent ground water, a
degassing apparatus may be required; follow manufacturer’s
instructions.
X 	During well development—Monitor turbidity caused by well
installation, recording consecutive measurements to document
decreases in turbidity as development proceeds.
X 	During well purging—Monitor changes in turbidity by taking
sequential readings until purging criteria are met (NFM 6.0).
The final stabilized turbidity value should be equal to or less
than the value recorded at the end of well development. A
decrease in turbidity values during purging can indicate
mitigation of subsurface disturbance caused by well installation
and by deployment of data-collection equipment in the well.
X 	For dynamic measurement—Report the median of the three or
more sequential measurements that meet the ±10-percent
criterion for stability (NFM 6.0).
X 	For discrete-sample measurement using a turbidimeter or
spectrophotometer:
— 	Bailers are not recommended for collecting turbidity
samples, as bailer deployment can increase turbidity.
— 	Do not collect the discharge passing through the
flowthrough chamber in which pH, conductivity, or other
field-measurement sensors are installed.
5Diluted samples must be qualified with a “d” in the “Value Qualifier Code” field when entering
data into NWIS.

turns.question: So can we just flag anything over 19 NTU as a problem at our well pods?
turns.answer:
I don’t have a configured threshold for your pod, so I can’t confirm a specific “flag‑over‑19 NTU” rule for this deployment.  

The USGS notes that “Natural ground‑water turbidity of up to 19 turbidity units has been reported”【1†"Natural ground‑water turbidity of up to 19 turbidity units has been reported"】, indicating that values above 19 NTU are higher than the natural range documented in that source. However, the excerpt does not define anything above 19 NTU as a problem or prescribe a flagging action.
